meta.subtitle: Network-on-chip IP licensor scaling ACV and royalties while GAAP losses persist

analystCommentary: We rate Arteris {+ BUY +} with a $28–$42 target range against a $24.78 share price. The case rests on three facts from the June 2026 quarter: revenue reached $24.1 million, up 46% year over year; annual contract value plus royalties climbed to $99.5 million, up 44%; and the company stayed GAAP-unprofitable, with an operating loss of $13.9 million. Growth is bought with heavy research and sales spending, so the trailing P/E is negative at -28.5x and the stock changes hands at 14.4x trailing sales. The bull case is a royalty inflection as design wins reach production; the bear case is a de-rating of a richly valued, loss-making small-cap. Consensus is more positive than we are, with a $39.43 average target implying +59.1% and a unanimous seven-analyst Buy. We size the modeled upside against a real bear at $17 and settle on Buy rather than a stronger call, because the path to profitability is still a FY27 event.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: Arteris, Inc. provides semiconductor system intellectual property, centered on network-on-chip (NoC) interconnect IP that manages on-chip communication in system-on-chip designs and systems of chiplets. Its product families include FlexGen, FlexNoC and FlexWay non-coherent NoC IP, the Ncore cache-coherent NoC, and the CodaCache last-level cache; it also sells Cycuity hardware-security verification software and the Magillem and CSRCompiler integration-automation tools, alongside professional services, support and maintenance. Arteris licenses this IP to chip and system makers across the automotive, communications, enterprise-computing, consumer-electronics and industrial markets, and earns variable royalties as its customers' chips ship. The company was founded in 2003 and is headquartered in Campbell, California. It generated $70.6 million of revenue in FY25, up 22.3%, at a 90.2% gross margin, but it has never reported a GAAP profit: FY25 brought a net loss of $34.7 million and diluted EPS of -$0.82. The model is subscription-and-royalty in shape, so reported revenue lags bookings; management tracks annual contract value plus royalties and remaining performance obligation as the leading indicators of that backlog.

thesis.body: The thesis is that Arteris is compounding its contracted revenue base quickly enough to grow into a demanding valuation, but not yet quickly enough to remove the risk in owning a loss-making name. Bookings and revenue are still growing at double-digit rates, yet the shares change hands at a full, software-like multiple of sales while GAAP losses continue, so the price already discounts several more years of execution. Our $28–$42 target range brackets a base case a little above today's $24.78 price, and the reward-to-risk we model is below one, which is why our rating is Buy and not something more emphatic.

catalysts: Royalty inflection: trailing royalties are growing faster than license revenue and should build further as design wins reach volume production.
Backlog conversion: a large and growing remaining performance obligation underwrites the multi-year revenue estimate.
Design-win momentum: a rising pace of confirmed design starts, most now embedding AI compute, feeds the future royalty pool.
Path to profit: consensus has Arteris crossing to GAAP profitability in FY27.
A new finance chief, Saurabh Sinha, joined from Aeva Technologies, bringing public-company experience as the model scales.
risks: Profitability is still years out: the quarter ran a GAAP operating loss and an operating margin near {- -58% -}, so the equity depends on future royalties, not current earnings.
Valuation risk: on consensus FY27 earnings the stock trades at roughly 199.4x forward earnings, leaving little room for a stumble.
Competition: the filing names Arm and Cadence as better-resourced rivals, and warns that customers can develop interconnect IP in-house.
Concentration and geography: the business leans on a limited set of large design wins and on customers in China, exposing it to trade, tariff and export-control shifts.
Dilution: the share count keeps rising as Arteris funds itself with equity, most recently around 49.15 million shares outstanding.

financials.incomeCommentary: Revenue in the June 2026 quarter was $24.1 million, up 46% year over year, split across licensing, support and maintenance, variable royalties, and a newly meaningful professional-services line. Growth is not the problem; spending is. Operating expenses outran gross profit and produced a GAAP operating loss of $13.9 million, wider than the $8.2 million loss a year earlier, and the quarter also absorbed acquisition-related costs from a deal that closed earlier in the year. On a non-GAAP basis, which the company reports to exclude acquisition-related and other items, the operating loss was $4.6 million against $3.5 million a year earlier, so the underlying loss widened far less than the GAAP figure. Net loss was $14.1 million, or $0.30 per share, versus a non-GAAP net loss of $4.7 million, or $0.10 per share. Gross margin remains the model's strength, at 87.6% on a trailing-twelve-month basis. For the full year, consensus sees revenue near $96.7 million, up about 37%, with a narrower loss of $0.18 per share before a first profit in FY27.
financials.balanceCommentary: Arteris ended FY25 with $33.9 million of cash and cash equivalents; the vendor tearsheet files that same figure under a cash-and-short-term-investments label, but the filing shows short-term investments reported separately on top, so we use the filing's narrower cash figure here. After years of losses, total equity was negative at -$14.6 million at the FY25 year-end. By mid-2026 the balance sheet was materially stronger: shares outstanding and additional paid-in capital had risen, cash had increased, and total stockholders' equity had turned positive. Liquidity is adequate, with a trailing-twelve-month current ratio of 1.57, up from 1.13 at the FY25 year-end. The most important balance-sheet line for a licensing model is the backlog: remaining performance obligation of $135 million, up 36% year over year, is contracted revenue that will convert to the income statement over time. The company carries no meaningful financial debt, so leverage is not a concern; the risk on this balance sheet is dilution, not solvency.
financials.cashflowCommentary: Cash generation is the quiet good-news story. Free cash flow turned positive in FY25 at $5.3 million, a swing to a 7.6% free-cash-flow margin from years of cash burn. The subscription model, which collects cash as deferred revenue ahead of recognition, structurally favors cash conversion, though the pack does not isolate that as the driver of the FY25 swing. Capital intensity is low, with FY25 capital expenditure of just -$1.4 million, so operating cash converts efficiently. Management guides full-year 2026 free cash flow to $5.0 million to $9.0 million and has stopped giving quarterly free-cash-flow guidance. On a trailing basis the free-cash-flow yield is only 0.6%, a reminder that the market is paying for growth rather than for current cash returns. There is no dividend and no buyback; every dollar is reinvested in research, sales and the recent acquisition.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: Traditional earnings multiples do not work here: with GAAP losses the trailing P/E is -28.5x and the next-twelve-month P/E is -141.0x, both meaningless as anchors. The cleaner gauge is price to sales, at 14.4x trailing revenue, a software-like multiple for a company still scaling. On the year GAAP profit is first expected, the forward P/E is roughly 199.4x, so the market is valuing FY27 earnings power, not FY26. There is no positive EBITDA, so EV/EBITDA is not available. We anchor instead on revenue growth and the contracted backlog. The Street is unanimous and more optimistic than we are: seven analysts rate the stock Buy, with a consensus target of $39.43, a median of $40.00 and a range of $30.00 to $50.00. Rather than lean on a peer multiples table, we note that the filing's own named competitors, Arm and Cadence, are far larger and better capitalized, which is a reason to require a valuation cushion, not to pay up.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Annual contract value plus royalties and remaining performance obligation keep compounding at better than 40% a year, variable royalties inflect as design wins reach volume production, and non-GAAP operating losses close toward breakeven ahead of the FY27 GAAP crossover. A market willing to pay a premium for durable IP growth pushes the shares back toward their prior 52-week high of $50.26.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Revenue grows in line with consensus, near $96.7 million in FY26 and $117 million in FY27, GAAP losses persist in the near term but free cash flow stays modestly positive, and the stock re-rates only a little above today's price as solid bookings growth is offset by an already-rich sales multiple.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Design-win timing slips, the royalty ramp underwhelms, and pricing pressure from larger rivals compresses the growth rate just as a risk-off market stops paying up for unprofitable growth. The multiple contracts hard and the shares fall back to the high teens, around $17, well above the $9.46 52-week low but a painful drawdown from here.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: We weight the base case at 45%, the bear at 30% and the bull at 25%, reflecting a genuine growth story tempered by a rich price and a still-distant profit. The bull implies $49, roughly the prior high; the base implies $31, modestly above the current quote; the bear implies $17. That spread leaves the probability-weighted fair value above today's price, but with a bear drawdown deep enough that the reward-to-risk sits under one. Our $28 to $42 target range brackets the base case and marks where we think the shares can reasonably trade over the coming year. The rating is Buy on the balance of these outcomes, held one notch below the Street's unanimous stronger stance because profitability is a FY27, not a FY26, event.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: Arteris reports as a single operating and reportable segment, so there is no product or geographic revenue split to analyze; the whole company is the unit. Within that single segment, revenue comes in three forms: licensing, support and maintenance, the core recurring component; variable royalties earned as customers ship chips that embed Arteris IP; and professional services. The IP itself spans the FlexNoC, FlexGen and FlexWay network-on-chip families, the Ncore cache-coherent interconnect, the CodaCache last-level cache, the Cycuity hardware-security tools and the Magillem and CSRCompiler integration-automation software. End markets are diversified across automotive, communications, enterprise computing, consumer electronics and industrial, with enterprise computing averaging 29% of annual contract value plus royalties over the past four quarters as data-center and chiplet design activity has grown.

moatFactors.name: Design-in switching costs
moatFactors.body: Once an interconnect IP is architected into a system-on-chip, replacing it means re-verifying the whole design, so customers rarely switch mid-generation. That lock-in is what converts a license today into variable royalties for years as the chip ships, and it underpins the remaining performance obligation the company carries.

moatFactors.name: Proprietary IP and patents
moatFactors.body: The value is codified in patented NoC and cache-coherency technology and in security-verification tools such as Cycuity, which are hard to replicate and which larger partners license rather than rebuild; Arm's decision to license Arteris hardware-security technology is evidence of that pull.

moatFactors.name: Recurring, contracted revenue
moatFactors.body: The subscription-and-royalty model produces contracted backlog and a high, software-like gross margin, giving revenue visibility uncommon for a company this size, though the base is still small in absolute dollars.

moatFactors.name: Scale versus incumbents
moatFactors.body: The countervailing factor is size: the filing names Arm and Cadence as rivals with far greater financial and engineering resources, and customers can build interconnect in-house, which caps pricing power and keeps the moat narrow rather than wide.

businessMoat.durability: The moat should widen slowly if the royalty base compounds, because each design win that reaches production adds annuity-like revenue that is expensive for a customer to unwind. The same forces that make the IP sticky, though, also make growth lumpy: revenue is gated by customers' design cycles, which run for years, and by their end products reaching volume. Durability therefore depends less on any single quarter than on the breadth of new design starts and on Arteris staying ahead technically of much larger competitors. We judge the moat narrow and improving, not wide: the switching costs are real, but the company is not yet large or profitable enough to be insulated from a well-resourced competitive response.

points: Royalties are the operating leverage in the model: trailing variable royalties of $8.6 million grew 65% year over year, faster than license revenue, and each design that reaches volume production adds annuity-like royalty income on top of the original license fee.

Design starts are the leading indicator of that future royalty pool: confirmed starts rose 21% over the trailing twelve months, management says most new designs now embed AI compute, and today's wins seed revenue several years out as those chips tape out and ship.

The contracted base is growing ahead of reported revenue: annual contract value plus royalties and remaining performance obligation are both expanding by double digits, and the pace at which that backlog converts to recognized revenue as subscriptions renew and chips ship is the number to watch.

Guidance frames the near-term ramp: full-year 2026 revenue is guided to $95.0 million to $98.0 million, with consensus modeling a step up to $117 million in FY27 as royalties build toward a first GAAP profit.

management.leadership: Arteris is led by K. Charles Janac, its President and Chief Executive Officer and a member of the Board. The notable recent change is in the finance seat: Saurabh Sinha joined as Chief Financial Officer on September 8, 2026, from Aeva Technologies, where the release says he helped take the company public and ran capital allocation and investor relations; he succeeds Nick Hawkins in the role. The incoming CFO brings public-company financial experience useful as Arteris scales toward profitability, and the finance transition is the main leadership item for investors to track. The board and executive group is small, consistent with a company of this size, and the company was founded in 2003.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation is entirely growth-oriented. Arteris pays no dividend and runs no buyback; internally generated cash is reinvested in research and development and sales, the two lines that drive the operating loss. The company funds the remaining gap with equity, evident in the rising share count and paid-in capital through mid-2026. It also deployed capital on an acquisition earlier in the year, which lifted goodwill and intangibles and carried one-time deal costs through operating expense. Free cash flow turned positive in FY25 at $5.3 million and is guided to $5.0 million to $9.0 million for the year, so reinvestment is no longer wholly funded by dilution, though equity issuance remains the swing source of capital for now.
management.governance: Governance rests on the April 2026 proxy statement, which discloses beneficial ownership and related-party dealings but not, in the excerpt available, detailed board-independence data. Control is concentrated: entities and individuals tied to CEO Janac, chiefly Bayview Legacy, LLC, hold about 19.8% of the stock, and the related-party section describes the 2022 Transchip technology-license arrangement, a former subsidiary in China that was deconsolidated and in which Arteris retained roughly a 35.0% equity-method stake. Concentrated founder ownership aligns the CEO with shareholders but also limits outside influence over the board. The proxy does not, in this excerpt, provide enough to assess committee independence, so we flag that as a gap rather than a positive or a negative.
management.insiderOwnership: Insider and large-holder ownership is high. Directors and executive officers as a group hold 23.3% of the shares, and CEO Janac's combined interests come to roughly 20.0%, most of it through Bayview Legacy, LLC. Among outside investors, Needham Investment Management is disclosed as a 5%-or-greater holder at 7.2%. That concentration means a small group effectively sets the shareholder vote, which cuts both ways: it keeps management focused on long-term value, but it leaves minority holders with limited sway and can weigh on the stock's free float and trading liquidity.

idiosyncratic: History of losses and a long conversion cycle. Arteris has never earned a GAAP profit, and revenue is recognized well after a design is won, so the equity is a bet on royalties that arrive years after the sales effort and research spend that win them; if design wins fail to reach volume production, the invested cost is stranded.

Competition from far larger firms. The 10-Q names Arm and Cadence as competitors with greater financial, technical and engineering resources, and warns that customers may develop interconnect IP internally; either could compress pricing or slow design-win capture.

Customer and end-market concentration. Growth leans on a limited number of large design wins in cyclical semiconductor end markets, so a delay or loss at one major customer can swing results and the contracted backlog.

China and trade-policy exposure. The company depends on international customers, calls out risks of doing business in China, and is exposed to tariffs, export controls and sanctions that could restrict its ability to sell to or collect from customers in certain regions.

Concentrated ownership and a related-party legacy. Founder-linked entities control roughly a fifth of the stock, and the Transchip arrangement leaves a China-based equity-method stake on the books, both of which complicate governance.
risks.systemic: The systemic risks are the ones every unprofitable, richly valued growth stock carries into a tightening or risk-off market. Higher discount rates hit long-duration equities like this one hardest, because most of the value sits in profits several years out; a market that stops paying premium sales multiples would compress the stock regardless of company execution. Arteris is also geared to the semiconductor cycle: its royalties rise and fall with its customers' chip shipments, so a broad downturn in end demand across automotive, data center and consumer electronics would slow both bookings and royalties at once. Tariffs and geopolitical friction, particularly between the United States and China, sit on top as a macro overhang the company cannot control.

body: Our call on Arteris is Buy, with a fair-value band of $28 to $42. The company is converting a fast-growing base of design wins into contracted, recurring revenue, and its royalty stream, the operating leverage in the model, is compounding faster than licenses as chips reach production. High gross margins and free cash flow that has turned positive already set it apart from most cash-burning small-caps.

The reason we stop at Buy rather than match the Street's unanimous stronger rating is price and timing. At a full, software-like multiple of sales with no current earnings, the stock already discounts years of flawless execution, and our upside only modestly outweighs the bear case, a de-rating to $17 that is a real outcome for a name that has already fallen by half from its 52-week high. What to watch: the trajectory of the non-GAAP operating loss toward breakeven, the pace of remaining performance obligation and design starts, and evidence that royalties are inflecting as chips ship.
